questions.q: What is Lebanon told to do?
questions.a: Lebanon is told to open its doors so that fire can burn up its cedar trees.

questions.q: What does the fall of the cedar trees cause the cypress trees to do?
questions.a: It causes the cypress trees to wail.
The shepherds are crying because their pastures have been destroyed.

questions.q: What did Yahweh tell Zechariah to do?
questions.a: Yahweh told Zechariah to shepherd the flock that was intended for slaughter.

questions.q: What do the sellers of the sheep say?
questions.a: The sellers say they praise Yahweh because they are becoming rich.

questions.q: What did Yahweh say he would do to the inhabitants of the land?
questions.a: Yahweh said he would no longer pity them, but would let each man’s neighbor and king dominate him, and they would destroy the land, and he would not rescue them.

questions.q: What were the names of the two staffs that Zechariah used to shepherd the flock meant for slaughter?
questions.a: The names of the two staffs were “Favor” and “Union.”

questions.q: Why did Zechariah destroy three shepherds in one month?
questions.a: Zechariah did this because he became impatient with the shepherds, and they also hated him.

questions.q: What did Zechariah say he would no longer do?
questions.a: Zechariah said he would no longer be their shepherd.

questions.q: Why did Zechariah break his staff, “Favor?”
questions.a: He broke it to break the covenant that he had made with all the peoples.

questions.q: What did the poor of the flock who were watching Zechariah know?
questions.a: They knew that it was the word of Yahweh.
Zechariah was paid thirty pieces of silver.

questions.q: What did Yahweh tell Zechariah to do with his thirty pieces of silver?
questions.a: Yahweh told him to throw it to the potter at the house of Yahweh.

questions.q: What did breaking the second staff, Union, do?
questions.a: Breaking the second staff broke the brotherhood between Judah and Israel.

questions.q: What did Yahweh tell Zechariah to take again?
questions.a: Yahweh told him to take the tools of a foolish shepherd.

questions.q: Yahweh said he would raise up a shepherd in the land. What will that shepherd do?
questions.a: That shepherd will not care for the sheep. He will not help the sheep that are perishing, he will not search for the ones that have strayed, and he will not heal the ones that are injured. He will not feed the healthy sheep, but will eat the fattest sheep and tear off their hooves.

questions.q: What curse is pronounced upon the worthless shepherd who forsakes the flock?
questions.a: The curse says that a sword will strike the shepherd’s arm and his right eye, and that his arm will wither and his right eye will become blind.

commentary.text: Destruction to come upon the Jews.
The Lord's dealing with the Jews.
The emblem and curse of a foolish shepherd.

Verses 1–3 In figurative expressions, that destruction of Jerusalem, and of the Jewish church and nation, is foretold, which our Lord Jesus, when the time was at hand, prophesied plainly and expressly. How can the fir trees stand, if the cedars fall? The falls of the wise and good into sin, and the falls of the rich and great into trouble, are loud alarms to those every way their inferiors. It is sad with a people, when those who should be as shepherds to them, are as young lions. The pride of Jordan was the thickets on the banks; and when the river overflowed the banks, the lions came up from them roaring. Thus the doom of Jerusalem may alarm other churches.

Christ came into this world for judgment to the Jewish church and nation, which were wretchedly corrupt and degenerate. Those have their minds wofully blinded, who do ill, and justify themselves in it; but God will not hold those guiltless who hold themselves so. How can we go to God to beg a blessing on unlawful methods of getting wealth, or to return thanks for success in them? There was a general decay of religion among them, and they regarded it not. The Good Shepherd would feed his flock, but his attention would chiefly be directed to the poor. As an emblem, the prophet seems to have taken two staves; Beauty, denoted the privileges of the Jewish nation, in their national covenant; the other he called Bands, denoting the harmony which hitherto united them as the flock of God. But they chose to cleave to false teachers. The carnal mind and the friendship of the world are enmity to God; and God hates all the workers of iniquity: it is easy to foresee what this will end in. The prophet demanded wages, or a reward, and received thirty pieces of silver. By Divine direction he cast it to the potter, as in disdain for the smallness of the sum. This shadowed forth the bargain of Judas to betray Christ, and the final method of applying it. Nothing ruins a people so certainly, as weakening the brotherhood among them. This follows the dissolving of the covenant between God and them: when sin abounds, love waxes cold, and civil contests follow. No wonder if those fall out among themselves, who have provoked God to fall out with them. Wilful contempt of Christ is the great cause of men's ruin. And if professors rightly valued Christ, they would not contend about little matters.

God, having showed the misery of this people in their being justly left by the Good Shepherd, shows their further misery in being abused by foolish shepherds. The description suits the character Christ gives of the scribes and Pharisees. They never do any thing to support the weak, or comfort the feeble-minded; but seek their own ease, while they are barbarous to the flock. The idol shepherd has the garb and appearance of a shepherd, receives submission, and is supported at much expense; but he leaves the flock to perish through neglect, or leads them to ruin by his example. This suits many in different churches and nations, but the warning had an awful fulfilment in the Jewish teachers. And while such deceive others to their ruin, they will themselves have the deepest condemnation.
